summary: This article explains how rubbing moves tiny charged bits called electrons, why charged things pull or push, why dry air brings more shocks, and how lightning is a giant spark.
introduce: Write the key term “atom” on the board and give pairs thirty seconds to guess what it means. Share a few guesses, then tell students to find the word in “Static Electricity: Sparks All Around” and check whether they were right.

keyTerms.def: one of the tiny pieces that everything is made of
a very small part of an atom that has a negative charge

challengeTerms.def: a tiny particle in the center of an atom that has a positive charge
the amount of water vapor in the air

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that static electricity is more useful than it is annoying? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Explain why a rubbed balloon sticks to a wall but two rubbed hairs push apart.
struggling: Pre-teach atom, electron, and attract with pictures or gestures, then let weak readers draw a quick picture for each term and use it in a short spoken sentence.
gifted: Ask strong readers to read a challenging version and write a short paragraph that uses proton, neutral, and humidity to teach the class one of the terms with their own example.
